name: Mahākassapa
summary: In the Chan account, the first patriarch, who smiled when the Buddha held up a flower on Vulture Peak and received the 'treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa' (Wumenguan case 6). (U42 contributes the Chan patriarchal role only.)
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 1.

name: Ānanda
summary: In the Chan account the second patriarch, who received the Dharma from Mahākāśyapa (the 'knock down the flagpole' exchange, Wumenguan case 22). (U42 contributes the Chan patriarchal role only.)
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. name: Vasubandhu (Posu Pantou 婆修盤頭), twenty-first Chan patriarch
summary: Twenty-first patriarch in the Chan list; the Chan biography (an ascetic who ate one meal a day) does not match the Yogācāra author (tch:vasubandhu), so a separate entry is kept.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. summary: Twenty-second patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. name: Siṃha / Āryasiṃha (Shizi 師子)
summary: Twenty-fourth patriarch in the Chan list; in the older Fu fazang yinyuan zhuan his execution by a king of Kashmir ended the transmission, whereas the Chan list continues it through Basiasita.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. name: Puṇyamitra (Buru Miduo 不如蜜多)
summary: Twenty-sixth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. name: Prajñātāra (Bore Duoluo 般若多羅)
summary: Twenty-seventh patriarch in the Chan list, teacher of Bodhidharma; the Platform Sūtra (10.32) cites his prophecy of a colt (Mazu) who would trample the world.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 27.

name: Bodhidharma (Putidamo 菩提達磨)

tradition.text: arrived 520 or 527 (Song accounts); died 536 or later, returned west with one sandal

realization_account.text: Heir of Prajñātāra in the 28-generation Indian line; brought the mind-seal east; 'wall-gazing Brahmin'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: First Chinese and twenty-eighth Indian patriarch of Chan. In the tradition's account a South Indian prince and disciple of Prajñātāra who came to China, told Emperor Wu of Liang that his merit was 'no merit' and the holy truth 'vast emptiness, nothing holy', sat facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin, and transmitted robe and Dharma to Huike. The earliest source (Xu gaoseng zhuan, 645) describes a South Indian brahmin teaching 'wall-gazing' and the four practices in the Northern Wei.

name: Huike 慧可 (Shenguang)

realization_account.text: 'I have searched for the mind and cannot find it.' — 'I have pacified your mind for you.' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 3; Wumenguan case 41).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Second Chinese patriarch. In the tradition's account he stood in the snow and cut off his own arm to show his resolve, asked Bodhidharma to pacify his mind and was told 'bring me the mind'; the earliest biography (Xu gaoseng zhuan) says bandits cut off his arm and that Bodhidharma gave him the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra.

name: Sengcan 僧璨
summary: Third patriarch. In the tradition's account a layman with a skin disease who asked Huike to absolve his sins and was told 'bring me your sins'; credited with the Xinxin ming. Historically obscure.

name: Daoxin 道信
summary: Fourth patriarch, who settled on Mount Shuangfeng (Huangmei) with a large community; taught 'guarding the one without moving' and the one-practice samādhi (Lengqie shizi ji). When a novice he asked Sengcan for liberation and was asked 'who binds you?'

name: Hongren 弘忍
summary: Fifth patriarch at the East Mountain (Huangmei); taught guarding the original true mind (Xiuxin yao lun); in the Platform Sūtra he set the verse contest and secretly transmitted robe and Dharma to Huineng.

name: Faru 法如
summary: Hongren's disciple at Shaolin, presented in early epitaphs and the Chuan fabao ji as his successor.

name: Lao'an (Hui'an 慧安)
summary: Long-lived disciple of Hongren honoured by Empress Wu.

name: Shenxiu 神秀 (Datong)
summary: Senior disciple of Hongren and founder of the Northern school; invited to the court by Empress Wu (701) and honoured as 'Dharma lord of the two capitals'. In the Platform Sūtra he writes the verse 'the body is the bodhi tree, the mind like a bright mirror's stand; wipe it constantly' and later sends Zhicheng to Huineng, praising Huineng's 'wisdom without a teacher'.

name: Puji 普寂
summary: Shenxiu's heir, leader of the Northern school in the capitals; the main target of Shenhui's attacks.

name: Yifu 義福
summary: Shenxiu's heir in Chang'an.

name: Xiangmo Zang 降魔藏
summary: Northern-school disciple of Shenxiu.

name: Jingjue 淨覺
summary: Northern-school author of the Lengqie shizi ji.

name: Du Fei 杜朏
summary: Lay author of the Chuan fabao ji.

name: Zhishen 智詵
summary: Hongren's disciple in Sichuan, founder of the Jingzhong line.

name: Chuji 處寂
summary: Jingzhong master, teacher of Musang.

name: Musang 無相 (Kim heshang 金和尚)
summary: Korean prince-monk in Sichuan; taught 'no remembering, no thinking, no forgetting' as precepts, samādhi and wisdom, opening his assemblies with drawn-out recitation of the Buddha's name (Lidai fabao ji).

name: Wuzhu 無住
summary: Founder of the Baotang school in Chengdu; rejected ritual and recitation, teaching no-thought alone; claimed Bodhidharma's robe.

name: Niutou Farong 牛頭法融
summary: Founder of the Oxhead school on Mount Niutou; in the tradition's account visited by Daoxin, after which birds no longer brought him flowers. Credited with the Xinming and the Jueguan lun.

name: Niutou Zhiwei 牛頭智威
summary: Oxhead master in the lineage from Farong.

name: Helin Xuansu 鶴林玄素
summary: Oxhead master.

name: Jingshan Faqin 徑山法欽
summary: Oxhead master honoured at court; the tradition says Danxia and others visited him.

name: Huineng 惠能 / 慧能 (the Sixth Patriarch)

tradition.text: 638–713 (born 638, received the robe at 24, ordained at 39, taught 37 years — Platform Sūtra 13.18)

realization_account.text: On hearing 'one should produce a mind that abides nowhere' from the Diamond Sūtra he 'greatly awakened that all dharmas are not apart from the self-nature' and exclaimed that the self-nature is originally pure, unborn, complete, unmoving and able to produce all dharmas (Platform Sūtra 4.13).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Sixth and last patriarch. In the tradition's account an illiterate firewood seller from Lingnan who awoke on hearing the Diamond Sūtra, laboured pounding rice at Hongren's monastery, answered Shenxiu's verse with 'originally there is not a single thing', received robe and Dharma at night, hid among hunters for fifteen years, revealed himself at the wind-and-flag debate, and taught the sudden teaching at Caoxi; his body is preserved at Nanhua temple. Scholars see him as a historical but obscure southern teacher whose image was shaped by Shenhui and the Platform Sūtra.

name: Fahai 法海
summary: Huineng's disciple, named as recorder of the Platform Sūtra.

name: Zongbao 宗寶
summary: Yuan-dynasty monk of Guangzhou who edited the standard edition of the Platform Sūtra (1291).

name: Heze Shenhui 荷澤神會
summary: Disciple of Huineng who at the Huatai assembly (732) and in Luoyang attacked the Northern school as collateral and gradual and proclaimed Huineng the true Sixth Patriarch; raised funds for the state by ordinations during the An Lushan rebellion; in 796 an imperial commission recognised him as seventh patriarch. In the Zongbao Platform Sūtra Huineng calls him a mere 'follower of intellectual understanding'.

name: Dugu Pei 獨孤沛
summary: Recorder of Shenhui's Huatai debate.

name: Guifeng Zongmi 圭峰宗密
summary: Fifth Huayan patriarch who considered himself an heir of Shenhui's Heze line; classified the Chan schools, taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation and the mind's 'empty and calm knowing', and criticised Hongzhou. (Owned by U54; U42 contributes the Chan role.)

name: Nanyue Huairang 南嶽懷讓
summary: Disciple of Huineng ('to call it a thing misses the mark'), teacher of Mazu; polished a tile to show that sitting does not make a buddha.

name: Qingyuan Xingsi 青原行思
summary: Disciple of Huineng who 'did not even practise the holy truths'; teacher of Shitou; ancestor of the Caodong, Yunmen and Fayan houses.

name: Yongjia Xuanjue 永嘉玄覺
summary: Tiantai-trained monk said to have been confirmed by Huineng after one night ('the one-night guest'); credited with the Zhengdao ge and the Yongjia ji.

name: Wei Jing 魏靜
summary: Compiler of the Yongjia ji.

name: Nanyang Huizhong 南陽慧忠 (National Teacher Zhong)
summary: Disciple of Huineng and teacher to emperors; taught that the insentient preach the Dharma, criticised 'southern' teachers who held that the body perishes while the mind-nature is eternal, and is said to have originated the circle-figures.

name: Danyuan Yingzhen 耽源應真
summary: Attendant of Huizhong who passed the 97 circle-figures to Yangshan (Rentian yanmu).

name: Mazu Daoyi 馬祖道一

realization_account.text: Sitting in meditation to become a buddha, he was asked by Huairang, who polished a tile, 'can polishing a tile make a mirror? can sitting in meditation make a buddha?' and awoke on hearing the instruction (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 5).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Hongzhou school; taught that 'this very mind is buddha', 'neither mind nor buddha' and that 'the ordinary mind is the Way'; his teaching style of shouts, blows and everyday gestures began encounter dialogue; over 130 heirs are recorded.

name: Shitou Xiqian 石頭希遷
summary: Heir of Qingyuan in Hunan, author of the Cantongqi; with Mazu one of the 'two great masters' of the later 8th c. — 'Jiangxi is ruled by Daji, Hunan by Shitou'.

name: Tianhuang Daowu 天皇道悟
summary: Heir of Shitou (also studied with Mazu), ancestor via Longtan of Deshan and Xuefeng.

name: Longtan Chongxin 龍潭崇信
summary: Heir of Tianhuang; blew out Deshan's candle, whereupon Deshan awoke.

name: Baizhang Huaihai 百丈懷海
summary: Heir of Mazu, credited by the tradition with founding independent Chan monasteries and the monastic rule; 'a day without work, a day without food'; his fox kōan.

name: Guling Shenzan 古靈神贊
summary: Heir of Baizhang who taught his former teacher by proclaiming Baizhang's 'the numinous light shines alone, free of senses and objects'.

name: Nanquan Puyuan 南泉普願
summary: Heir of Mazu; 'the ordinary mind is the Way'; killed the cat when the monks could not answer; teacher of Zhaozhou.

name: Damei Fachang 大梅法常
summary: Heir of Mazu who awoke at 'this very mind is buddha' and kept to it when Mazu switched to 'neither mind nor buddha'; Mazu said 'the plum is ripe'.

name: Xitang Zhizang 西堂智藏
summary: Heir of Mazu; teacher of the Korean founders Doui, Hongcheok and Hyecheol.

name: Dazhu Huihai 大珠慧海
summary: Heir of Mazu, author of the Dunwu rudao yaomen lun; 'I have no treasure — your own treasure house is complete'.

name: Guizong Zhichang 歸宗智常
summary: Heir of Mazu; cut a snake in two with his hoe (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 7).

name: Layman Pang (Pang Yun 龐蘊)
summary: Lay practitioner who studied with Shitou and Mazu; 'supernatural power and wondrous function: carrying water and hauling firewood'.

name: Danxia Tianran 丹霞天然
summary: Studied with Mazu and Shitou; burned a wooden buddha for warmth — 'I am burning it for relics'.

name: Yaoshan Weiyan 藥山惟儼
summary: Heir of Shitou; asked what he thought while sitting, answered 'thinking of not-thinking… non-thinking' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 14).

name: Yunyan Tansheng 雲巖曇晟
summary: Heir of Yaoshan and teacher of Dongshan; 'just this is it'.

name: Huangbo Xiyun 黃檗希運
summary: Heir of Baizhang; taught the one mind and no-mind to Pei Xiu (Chuanxin fayao, Wanling lu); struck Linji three times when asked the meaning of the buddha-dharma.

name: Pei Xiu 裴休
summary: Tang chief minister and lay disciple of Zongmi and Huangbo; recorded Huangbo's teaching.

name: Gao'an Dayu 高安大愚
summary: Heir of Guizong; at his words Linji awoke and exclaimed 'there isn't much to Huangbo's buddha-dharma'.

name: Linji Yixuan 臨濟義玄

realization_account.text: Three times he asked Huangbo the great meaning of the buddha-dharma and three times was struck; sent to Dayu and told Huangbo had been 'grandmotherly', he awoke and said 'there isn't much to Huangbo's buddha-dharma' (Linji lu, record of pilgrimage).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Linji house in Zhenzhou (Hebei); heir of Huangbo. Taught the true person of no rank, independence from all names, 'be master wherever you are', and used the shout; his sayings are the Linji lu.

name: Puhua 普化
summary: Eccentric companion of Linji who rang a bell in the streets; claimed as founder by the Japanese Fuke school.

name: Sansheng Huiran 三聖慧然
summary: Disciple of Linji named as compiler of the Linji lu.

name: Xinghua Cunjiang 興化存獎
summary: Heir of Linji through whom the main Linji line continued.

name: Nanyuan Huiyong 南院慧顒
summary: Linji master (d. c. 952).

name: Fengxue Yanzhao 風穴延沼
summary: Linji master who kept the line alive in the 10th c.

name: Shoushan Shengnian 首山省念
summary: Linji master; the 'bamboo staff' case (Wumenguan 43).

name: Fenyang Shanzhao 汾陽善昭
summary: Linji master who composed verses on old cases (songgu), a precursor of the kōan collections.

name: Shishuang Chuyuan (Ciming) 石霜楚圓
summary: Linji master, teacher of both Yangqi and Huanglong.

name: Zhaozhou Congshen 趙州從諗
summary: Heir of Nanquan who taught for forty years in old age; famed for his 'wu' to 'does a dog have buddha-nature?', 'the cypress in front of the hall', 'wash your bowl', 'have some tea'.

name: Juzhi 俱胝 (One-Finger Juzhi)
summary: Answered every question by raising one finger ('one-finger Chan' received from Tianlong), cut off a boy's imitating finger (Wumenguan case 3).

name: Guishan Lingyou 溈山靈祐
summary: Heir of Baizhang and co-founder of the Guiyang house; taught that one who awakens suddenly to principle must still gradually remove habit energies.

name: Yangshan Huiji 仰山慧寂
summary: Heir of Guishan and co-founder of the Guiyang house; received and burned the book of 97 circle-figures, having understood them.

name: Xiangyan Zhixian 香嚴智閑

realization_account.text: While sweeping, a pebble struck bamboo and at the sound he awoke; verse beginning 'one strike and I forgot all I knew; no further need of cultivation' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 11).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Learned monk who could not answer Guishan and burned his notes; later awoke when a pebble he swept struck a bamboo: 'one strike and I forgot all I knew'.

name: Lingyun Zhiqin 靈雲志勤

realization_account.text: 'Since once seeing the peach blossoms, until now I have had no more doubt' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 11).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Awoke on seeing peach blossoms after thirty years of seeking; Guishan confirmed him: 'one who awakens through conditions never regresses'.

name: Dongshan Liangjie 洞山良价

realization_account.text: Crossing a stream he saw his reflection and awoke, composing 'Do not seek it from others… I now go on alone and meet it everywhere; it now is me, I now am not it' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 15).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Co-founder of the Caodong house; heir of Yunyan; questioned the preaching of the insentient, awoke on seeing his reflection while crossing a stream, and taught the five ranks and the Precious Mirror Samādhi.

name: Caoshan Benji 曹山本寂
summary: Heir of Dongshan and co-founder of the Caodong house; elaborated the five ranks as lord and minister.

name: Yunju Daoying 雲居道膺
summary: Heir of Dongshan through whom the Caodong line continued.

name: Shishuang Qingzhu 石霜慶諸
summary: Master who asked 'how do you step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole?' (Wumenguan case 46).

name: Deshan Xuanjian 德山宣鑒
summary: Diamond-Sūtra scholar who burned his commentaries after awakening when Longtan blew out his candle; known for the stick ('thirty blows').

name: Xuefeng Yicun 雪峰義存
summary: Heir of Deshan in Fujian with a huge community; ancestor of the Yunmen and Fayan houses.

name: Xuansha Shibei 玄沙師備
summary: Heir of Xuefeng; 'the whole ten-direction world is one bright pearl'.

name: Luohan Guichen (Dizang) 羅漢桂琛
summary: Heir of Xuansha; told Fayan 'not knowing is most intimate'.

name: Fayan Wenyi 法眼文益
summary: Founder of the Fayan house in Nanjing; used Huayan categories; wrote the Ten Guidelines criticising faults of Chan teachers.

name: Tiantai Deshao 天台德韶
summary: Heir of Fayan and National Teacher of Wuyue; helped recover Tiantai texts from Korea.

name: Yongming Yanshou 永明延壽
summary: Heir of Deshao; compiled the Zongjing lu harmonising Chan and the teachings and advocated combining Chan with Pure Land practice; counted as a Pure Land patriarch.

name: Muzhou Daoming (Chen Zunsu) 睦州道明
summary: Heir of Huangbo who broke Yunmen's leg in a slammed gate, causing his awakening.

name: Yunmen Wenyan 雲門文偃

realization_account.text: When Muzhou slammed his gate on Yunmen's leg, breaking it, Yunmen awoke (tradition's account; Biyan lu case 6 commentary).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Yunmen house in Guangdong; heir of Xuefeng; known for one-word answers ('every day is a good day', 'a dried shit-stick').

name: Deshan Yuanmi 德山緣密
summary: Heir of Yunmen who divided his statement into the three phrases (Rentian yanmu).

name: Dongshan Shouchu 洞山守初
summary: Heir of Yunmen; answered 'three pounds of flax' to 'what is buddha?' (Biyan lu 12; Wumenguan 18). Distinct from Dongshan Liangjie.

name: Xianglin Chengyuan 香林澄遠
summary: Heir of Yunmen in Sichuan; ancestor of Xuedou.

name: Xuedou Chongxian 雪竇重顯
summary: Yunmen-house poet-master whose verses on a hundred cases formed the core of the Blue Cliff Record.

name: Mingjiao Qisong 明教契嵩
summary: Yunmen-house scholar-monk who defended the 28-patriarch lineage and the harmony of Buddhism with Confucianism.

name: Tanlin 曇林
summary: Disciple of Bodhidharma who recorded the Two Entrances with a preface.

name: Daoyu 道育
summary: With Huike one of Bodhidharma's two disciples named in the Xu gaoseng zhuan.

name: Na Chanshi 那禪師 and Huiman 慧滿
summary: Huike's disciples who carried the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra as the essence of mind (Xu gaoseng zhuan juan 16).

name: Daoxuan 道宣
summary: Vinaya master and historian, author of the Xu gaoseng zhuan with the earliest Bodhidharma and Huike biographies.

name: Zanning 贊寧
summary: Author of the Song gaoseng zhuan (988).

name: Daoyuan 道原
summary: Compiler of the Jingde chuandeng lu (1004), in the Fayan line.

name: Zhiju 智炬
summary: Compiler of the Baolin zhuan (801).

name: Moheyan 摩訶衍 (Hwashang Mahāyāna)
summary: Chinese Chan master at the Tibetan court whose teaching of not thinking and not examining was opposed by Kamalaśīla in the Samye debate; the Chinese record is the Dunwu dasheng zhengli jue. (U42 contributes the Chan side; the debate is dsp:sudden-or-gradual, U50.)
notes: Scholars link his teaching to Northern-school lines; the tradition's (Tibetan) accounts say he lost the debate, the Chinese record says he won.

name: Wangxi 王錫
summary: Compiler of the Chinese record of Moheyan's replies.

name: Fu Dashi 傅大士 (Fu Xi)
summary: Lay bodhisattva of the Liang honoured in Chan anecdotes and credited with verses such as the Xinwang ming (in Jingde chuandeng lu juan 30).

name: Baozhi 寶誌
summary: Wonder-working monk at the Liang court who, in the tradition's account, told Emperor Wu that Bodhidharma was Avalokiteśvara transmitting the buddha-mind seal (Biyan lu case 1).

name: Emperor Wu of Liang (Liang Wudi 梁武帝)
summary: Buddhist emperor (r. 502–549) who, in the tradition's account, asked Bodhidharma about the merit of his temple-building and was told 'no merit'.

name: Yangqi Fanghui 楊岐方會
summary: Founder of the Yangqi branch of the Linji house.

name: Huanglong Huinan 黃龍慧南
summary: Founder of the Huanglong branch; posed the 'three barriers' (Buddha's hand, donkey's leg, birth-conditions).

name: Huitang Zuxin 晦堂祖心
summary: Heir of Huanglong.

name: Donglin Changzong 東林常總
summary: Heir of Huanglong at Mount Lu, teacher of the poet Su Shi (Su Dongpo), whose awakening verse on the valley stream Dōgen cites.

name: Juefan Huihong 覺範慧洪
summary: Huanglong-branch scholar-poet who championed 'lettered Chan' (wenzi Chan).

name: Xu'an Huaichang 虛庵懷敞
summary: Huanglong-branch master at Mount Tiantai who gave Eisai the Linji transmission (1191).

name: Baiyun Shouduan 白雲守端
summary: Heir of Yangqi, teacher of Wuzu Fayan.

name: Doushuai Congyue 兜率從悅
summary: Huanglong-branch master who posed the 'three barriers of Doushuai' (Wumen guan case 47).

name: Wuzu Fayan 五祖法演
summary: Yangqi master at Mount Wuzu who used Zhaozhou's 'wu' as a single-word barrier and posed 'Qiannü and her soul separated' (Wumenguan 35).

name: Yuanwu Keqin 圜悟克勤
summary: Author of the Blue Cliff Record lectures; teacher of Dahui and Huqiu.

name: Dahui Zonggao 大慧宗杲

realization_account.text: On hearing Yuanwu quote 'a warm breeze comes from the south, and the palace pavilion grows slightly cool' he had a breakthrough, later deepened on the case 'being and non-being are like wisteria clinging to a tree' (tradition's account).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Heir of Yuanwu who systematised 'Chan of observing the phrase' (kanhua Chan): concentrate the great doubt on the critical phrase ('wu') throughout daily life until it shatters in awakening; denounced 'heretical silent-illumination Chan'. The tradition says he burned the Blue Cliff Record's printing blocks.

name: Zhuoan Deguang 拙庵德光
summary: Heir of Dahui who sent a certificate of transmission to Dainichi Nōnin's envoys (1189).

name: Huqiu Shaolong 虎丘紹隆
summary: Heir of Yuanwu from whom most later Linji and Japanese Rinzai lines descend.

name: Mi'an Xianjie 密庵咸傑
summary: Yangqi master in Huqiu's line.

name: Songyuan Chongyue 松源崇嶽
summary: Yangqi master in Huqiu's line; 'why does the person of great strength not lift his legs?' (Wumenguan 20).

name: Wuzhun Shifan 無準師範
summary: Abbot of Jingshan, teacher of Enni Ben'en and of several Chinese masters who went to Japan.

name: Xutang Zhiyu 虛堂智愚
summary: Yangqi master whose Japanese heir Nanpo Shōmyō began the Ōtōkan line.

name: Wumen Huikai 無門慧開
summary: Compiler of the Gateless Barrier; said to have worked on 'wu' for six years and awakened on hearing the drum for the midday meal.

name: Mixian Zongshao 彌衍宗紹
summary: Disciple who compiled the Wumen guan.

name: Xueyan Zuqin 雪巖祖欽
summary: Yangqi master; 'small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening' (Changuan cejin); teacher of Gaofeng.

name: Gaofeng Yuanmiao 高峰原妙
summary: Yuan-dynasty master of rigorous huatou practice who taught the three essentials of great faith, great doubt and great determination.

name: Zhongfeng Mingben 中峰明本
summary: Yuan master and hermit who advocated huatou practice and joint Chan–Pure Land practice.

name: Huiyan Zhizhao 晦巖智昭
summary: Compiler of the Rentian yanmu (1188).

name: Dayang Jingxuan 大陽警玄
summary: Caodong master who, having no heir, entrusted his robe to the Linji master Fushan Fayuan to pass to Touzi Yiqing.

name: Touzi Yiqing 投子義青
summary: Reviver of the Caodong line, received its transmission by proxy through Fushan Fayuan.

name: Furong Daokai 芙蓉道楷
summary: Caodong master known for austerity and refusal of imperial honours.

name: Danxia Zichun 丹霞子淳
summary: Caodong master, teacher of Hongzhi and Zhenxie.

name: Hongzhi Zhengjue 宏智正覺
summary: Caodong abbot of Tiantong for thirty years; taught silent illumination (mozhao) and wrote verses on a hundred cases (basis of the Book of Equanimity); friend of Dahui despite their disagreement.

name: Zhenxie Qingliao 真歇清了
summary: Caodong master in the Song, ancestor of Rujing's line; scholars suggest he may be among those Dahui criticised for 'silent illumination'.

name: Tiantong Rujing 天童如淨
summary: Caodong abbot of Tiantong and Dōgen's teacher; in Dōgen's account he taught that sitting is 'body and mind dropping off' and that just sitting suffices.

name: Wansong Xingxiu 萬松行秀
summary: Caodong master in the north (Jin/Yuan) who commented on Hongzhi's verses in the Book of Equanimity; teacher of Yelü Chucai.

name: Yelü Chucai 耶律楚材
summary: Khitan statesman under Chinggis Khan and lay disciple of Wansong, who asked for the Congrong lu and wrote its preface.

name: Changlu Zongze 長蘆宗賾
summary: Yunmen-line master and Pure Land devotee who compiled the Chanyuan qinggui (1103) with the Zuochan yi.

name: Dongyang Dehui 東陽德輝
summary: Abbot of Baizhangshan who compiled the imperial edition of the Pure Rules (1335–1338).

name: Li Zunxu 李遵勗
summary: Lay official who compiled the Tiansheng guangdeng lu (1036).

name: Dachuan Puji 大川普濟
summary: Compiler of the Wudeng huiyuan (1252).

name: Mu'an Shanqing 睦庵善卿
summary: Compiler of the Chan lexicon Zuting shiyuan (1108).

name: Yuanjue Zongyan 圓覺宗演
summary: Editor of the 1120 edition of the Linji lu.

name: Kuoan Shiyuan 廓庵師遠
summary: Song master (Liangshan) of the Yangqi line who composed the Ten Oxherding Pictures and verses.

name: Ciyuan 慈遠
summary: Disciple of Kuoan who wrote the prose prefaces to the Ten Oxherding Pictures.

name: Puming 普明
summary: Author of the alternative 'whitening ox' series of ten oxherding pictures; identity and date uncertain.

name: Yunqi Zhuhong 雲棲袾宏
summary: Ming reformer who combined Chan with Pure Land recitation ('who is it that recites the Buddha's name?') and compiled the Changuan cejin; counted a Pure Land patriarch.

name: Hanshan Deqing 憨山德清
summary: Ming master who restored Huineng's Caoxi monastery and advocated huatou practice and harmony of the three teachings.

name: Zibo Zhenke 紫柏真可
summary: Ming master who initiated the Jiaxing canon; died in prison.

name: Miyun Yuanwu 密雲圓悟
summary: Late-Ming Linji master at Tiantong who revived the use of shouts and blows; teacher of Feiyin.

name: Feiyin Tongrong 費隱通容
summary: Heir of Miyun, abbot of Wanfusi on Mount Huangbo, teacher of Yinyuan (Ingen).

name: Xuyun 虛雲
summary: Modern Chinese master who restored many monasteries (including Huineng's Nanhua) and is said to have held transmission in all five houses.

name: Doui 道義
summary: Silla monk who received Hongzhou Chan from Xitang Zhizang and returned in 821; founder of the Gajisan school and regarded by the modern Jogye Order as its founder.

name: Beomnang 法朗
summary: Silla monk said to have received Chan from the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin — the tradition's earliest Korean Seon link.

name: Hongcheok 洪陟
summary: Founder of the Silsangsan school, heir of Xitang Zhizang.

name: Hyecheol 慧哲
summary: Founder of the Dongnisan school, heir of Xitang Zhizang.

name: Muyeom 無染
summary: Founder of the Seongjusan school; heir of Magu Baoche.

name: Jinul 知訥 (Bojo)

realization_account.text: Three awakenings through texts rather than a living teacher: reading the Platform Sūtra (the self-nature is not defiled by the senses), Li Tongxuan's Huayan commentary, and Dahui's records (freedom from lingering obstruction).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Goryeo reformer of Seon: founded the Samādhi and Prajñā Community (Suseonsa, later Songgwangsa); taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation, tracing back the radiance to the empty and calm numinous awareness, the balanced cultivation of samādhi and prajñā, harmony with Huayan, and the hwadu as a shortcut.

name: Hyesim 慧諶 (Jingak guksa)
summary: Jinul's successor at Suseonsa, who promoted ganhwa Seon and compiled the Seonmun yeomsong jip.

name: Taego Bou 太古普愚
summary: Goryeo master who received Linji (Yangqi) transmission from Shiwu Qinggong in China (1348); regarded as reviver of the Jogye lineage and eponym of the Taego order.

name: Naong Hyegeun 懶翁慧勤
summary: Goryeo master who studied with Pingshan Chulin and the Indian monk Zhikong (Dhyānabhadra).

name: Hyujeong 休靜 (Seosan daesa)
summary: Joseon master who unified Seon and doctrinal study under ganhwa practice (Seon'ga gwigam) and led monk-soldiers against the Japanese invasion of 1592.

name: Samyeong Yujeong 四溟惟政
summary: Hyujeong's heir, monk-soldier and envoy to Japan.

name: Gyeongheo Seong'u 鏡虛惺牛
summary: Reviver of Korean Seon at the end of the Joseon dynasty, famed for unconventional conduct.

name: Mangong Wolmyeon 滿空月面
summary: Heir of Gyeongheo, influential teacher of ganhwa Seon in the 20th c.

name: Toeong Seongcheol 退翁性徹
summary: Supreme Patriarch of the Jogye Order who argued for sudden awakening/sudden cultivation against Jinul (Seonmun jeongno, 1981).

name: Myōan Eisai 明菴榮西 (Yōsai)
summary: Tendai monk who went to China twice (1168; 1187–1191), received the Huanglong Linji transmission from Xu'an Huaichang, founded Shōfukuji (Hakata) and Kenninji (Kyoto), wrote the Kōzen gokoku ron and Kissa yōjōki, and combined Zen with Tendai and esoteric practice and strict precepts.

name: Dainichi Nōnin 大日能忍
summary: Self-awakened founder of the Daruma school who obtained a certificate by proxy from Zhuoan Deguang; criticised by Eisai.

name: Kakuan 覺晏
summary: Nōnin's successor, teacher of Ejō.

name: Butsuju Myōzen 佛樹明全
summary: Eisai's disciple who went to China with Dōgen in 1223 and died at Tiantong in 1225.

name: Eihei Dōgen 永平道元

realization_account.text: During sitting at Tiantong, Rujing rebuked a dozing monk: 'practising Chan is body and mind dropping off'; hearing this Dōgen awoke and Rujing confirmed 'body and mind dropped off; dropped-off body and mind' (Sōtō biographies; Rujing xu yulu).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Japanese Sōtō: trained in Tendai and under Myōzen, went to China (1223–1227), received Caodong transmission from Tiantong Rujing, taught just sitting as the enactment of original realization, founded Kōshōji and Eiheiji, and wrote the Shōbōgenzō, Fukanzazengi and monastic instructions.

name: Koun Ejō 孤雲懷奘
summary: Former Daruma-school monk who became Dōgen's heir and second abbot of Eiheiji; recorded the Shōbōgenzō zuimonki.

name: Tettsū Gikai 徹通義介
summary: Third abbot of Eiheiji, teacher of Keizan.

name: Jakuen 寂圓
summary: Chinese disciple of Rujing who followed Dōgen to Japan and founded Hōkyōji.

name: Keizan Jōkin 瑩山紹瑾
summary: 'Second founder' of Sōtō: founded Yōkōji and Sōjiji, integrated esoteric and devotional rites, opened Sōtō to women and laity; author of the Denkōroku and Zazen yōjinki.

name: Gasan Jōseki 峨山韶碩
summary: Keizan's heir who spread Sōtō through his many disciples; said to have trained in the five ranks.

name: Manzan Dōhaku 卍山道白
summary: Tokugawa reformer who restored face-to-face, one-teacher dharma transmission (isshi inshō) in Sōtō.

name: Menzan Zuihō 面山瑞方
summary: Tokugawa scholar-monk who revived study of Dōgen's writings and wrote on precepts and zazen.

name: Taigu Ryōkan 大愚良寛
summary: Sōtō hermit-poet and calligrapher who lived as a mendicant in Echigo.

name: Kenzei 建撕
summary: Fourteenth abbot of Eiheiji, author of the Kenzeiki biography of Dōgen (1452).

name: Enni Ben'en 圓爾辨圓 (Shōichi kokushi)
summary: Heir of Wuzhun Shifan who founded Tōfukuji (Kyoto) and combined Zen with Tendai and esoteric teaching.

name: Lanxi Daolong 蘭溪道隆 (Rankei Dōryū)
summary: Chinese master who came to Japan (1246) and founded Kenchōji in Kamakura, introducing strict Song-style monastic Zen.

name: Wuxue Zuyuan 無學祖元 (Mugaku Sogen)
summary: Chinese master (heir of Wuzhun) invited by Hōjō Tokimune; founded Engakuji (1282).

name: Shinchi Kakushin 心地覺心 (Hottō kokushi)
summary: Studied under Wumen Huikai and brought the Wumen guan to Japan (1254); regarded by the Fuke school as its founder in Japan.

name: Nanpo Shōmyō 南浦紹明 (Daiō kokushi)
summary: Heir of Xutang Zhiyu; first of the Ōtōkan line (Ō-Tō-Kan: Daiō, Daitō, Kanzan) from which all present Rinzai lines descend.

name: Shūhō Myōchō 宗峰妙超 (Daitō kokushi)
summary: Heir of Nanpo, founder of Daitokuji; said to have lived twenty years among beggars under Kyoto's Gojō bridge after awakening.

name: Kanzan Egen 關山慧玄
summary: Heir of Daitō, founder of Myōshinji.

name: Musō Soseki 夢窓疎石
summary: Rinzai master and garden designer, adviser to the Ashikaga, founder of Tenryūji; author of Muchū mondō.

name: Ikkyū Sōjun 一休宗純
summary: Daitokuji-line eccentric poet-monk who satirised formal Zen; author of the Kyōunshū.

name: Bassui Tokushō 拔隊得勝
summary: Rinzai master who taught asking 'who is the master of seeing and hearing?' with great doubt.

name: Takuan Sōhō 澤庵宗彭
summary: Daitokuji abbot and adviser to the shogun; wrote on immovable wisdom for swordsmen.

name: Bankei Yōtaku 盤珪永琢

realization_account.text: Gravely ill after years of austerities, he spat a mass of black phlegm against a wall and at that moment realized that all things are perfectly resolved in the Unborn (Bankei's own account in his sermons).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Rinzai master who, after years of harsh practice and illness, realized that all things are resolved in the Unborn and taught in plain Japanese that everyone has the unborn buddha-mind.

name: Suzuki Shōsan 鈴木正三
summary: Former samurai turned monk who taught fierce 'guardian-king Zen', death contemplation and work in each occupation as buddha-practice.

name: Shōju Rōjin (Dōkyō Etan) 道鏡慧端
summary: Hermit master of the Ōtōkan line who humbled Hakuin after his first awakening and deepened his practice.

name: Hakuyū 白幽子 (Ishikawa Jishun)
summary: Hermit of the Kyoto hills who, in Hakuin's account, taught him the naikan and soft-butter methods to cure his Zen sickness.

name: Hakuin Ekaku 白隱慧鶴

realization_account.text: After days in great doubt, 'as if frozen in a sheet of ice', he broke through on hearing the distant sound of a temple bell (Eiganji, 1708); Shōju later rebuked his pride and he had further awakenings (Itsumadegusa).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Reviver of Japanese Rinzai: stressed great doubt, kenshō and post-awakening practice; introduced the kōan 'the sound of one hand'; recorded his Zen sickness and its cure (Yasenkanna); taught in vernacular writings and paintings; all living Rinzai lines descend from him.

name: Tōrei Enji 東嶺圓慈
summary: Hakuin's leading disciple and systematiser; author of the Shūmon mujintō ron.

name: Gasan Jitō 峨山慈棹
summary: Heir of Hakuin (via Gessen in some accounts) and teacher of Inzan and Takujū.

name: Inzan Ien 隱山惟琰
summary: Founder of one of the two branches (Inzan and Takujū) through which Hakuin's kōan curriculum is transmitted.

name: Takujū Kosen 卓洲胡僊
summary: Founder of the Takujū branch of the Hakuin kōan curriculum.

name: Ingen Ryūki 隱元隆琦 (Yinyuan Longqi)
summary: Chinese Linji master of Wanfusi (Mount Huangbo) who came to Nagasaki in 1654 and founded Manpukuji at Uji (1661), establishing the Ōbaku school.

name: Mokuan Shōtō 木庵性瑫
summary: Ingen's Chinese successor as abbot of Manpukuji.

name: Sokuhi Nyoitsu 即非如一
summary: Chinese Ōbaku master and calligrapher, founder of Fukujuji.

name: Tetsugen Dōkō 鐵眼道光
summary: Japanese Ōbaku monk who produced the woodblock edition of the complete canon (1669–1681), twice diverting the funds to famine relief first.

name: Moshan Liaoran 末山了然
summary: Tang nun, heir of Gao'an Dayu, the first woman recorded as a Chan master in the Jingde chuandeng lu; asked by Guanxi Zhixian what the master of Moshan is, she answered 'not a male or female form', and he served her three years as gardener.

name: Guanxi Zhixian 灌溪志閑
summary: Disciple of Linji who also served the nun Moshan Liaoran for three years.

name: Miaodao 妙道
summary: Song nun who awakened under Dahui's instruction and received his confirmation.

name: Wuzhuo Miaozong 無著妙總
summary: Song nun, recognised as one of Dahui's Dharma heirs; she later taught as abbess.

name: Mugai Nyodai 無外如大
summary: Kamakura-period nun, disciple of Wuxue Zuyuan, founder of the convent Keiaiji in Kyoto; regarded as the first Japanese woman Zen master.

name: Ryōnen Genso 了然元總
summary: Ōbaku nun and poet who, refused admission because of her beauty, is said to have scarred her face; later abbess.
notes: The face-scarring episode is recorded as the tradition's account; restricted-type austerity, summary only.
